title: Motion Introducing the Draft Constitution
topic: Form of Government, Federalism, and Fundamental Rights in the Draft Constitution
full_text:
Mr. Vice-President, Sir, I move that the Draft Constitution as framed by the Drafting Committee be taken into consideration. In doing so, I should like to draw the attention of the House to some of its salient features. A student of the Constitution would naturally ask: What is the form of government envisaged in the Draft Constitution? The Draft Constitution recommends a Parliamentary system of Government as in the United Kingdom, rather than the Presidential system as in America. In the Draft Constitution there is placed at the head of the Indian Union a functionary who is called the President of the Union. The title of this functionary reminds one of the President of the United States. But beyond identity of names there is nothing in common between the form of government prevalent in America and the form of government proposed under the Draft Constitution. The American form of government is called the Presidential system of government. What the Draft Constitution recommends is the Parliamentary system. The two are fundamentally different.

Under the Presidential system of the United States, the President is the chief head of the Executive. The administration is vested in him. Under the Draft Constitution, the President occupies the same position as the King under the English Constitution. He is the head of the State but not of the Executive. He represents the Nation but does not rule the Nation. He is the symbol of the nation. His place in the administration is that of a ceremonial device on a seal by which the nation's decisions are made known.

A democratic executive must satisfy two conditions - it must be a stable executive and it must be a responsible executive. Unfortunately, it has not been possible so far to devise a system which can ensure both in equal degree. You can have a system which can give you more stability but less responsibility, or you can have a system which gives you more responsibility but less stability. The American system gives more stability but less responsibility. The British system, on the other hand, gives you more responsibility but less stability. The Drafting Committee has preferred the system of daily assessment of responsibility to periodic assessment.
summary: Dr. Ambedkar introduces the Draft Constitution, elaborating why India chose the British Parliamentary executive over the American Presidential model: balancing stability with day-to-day executive accountability to the legislature.
key_quotes: The President is the head of the State but not of the Executive. He represents the Nation but does not rule the Nation.
A democratic executive must satisfy two conditions: stability and responsibility. The Drafting Committee preferred daily assessment of responsibility to periodic assessment.

title: Speech on the Third Reading of the Constitution (Grammar of Anarchy)
topic: Final Defense of the Constitution, Warnings on Hero-Worship, and Need for Social Democracy
full_text:
Sir, I look back upon the work of the Constituent Assembly with satisfaction. On 26th January 1950, India will be an independent country. What would happen to her independence? Will she maintain her independence or will she lose it again? This is the first thought that comes to my mind. It is not that India was never an independent country. The point is that she once lost the independence she had. Will she lose it a second time? What perturbs me greatly is the fact that not only India has once before lost her independence, but she lost it by the infidelity and treachery of some of her own people.

If we wish to maintain democracy not merely in form, but also in fact, what must we do? The first thing in my judgment we must do is to hold fast to constitutional methods of achieving our social and economic objectives. It means we must abandon the bloody methods of revolution. It means that we must abandon the method of civil disobedience, non-cooperation and satyagraha. When there was no way left for constitutional methods for achieving economic and social objectives, there was a great deal of justification for unconstitutional methods. But where constitutional methods are open, there can be no justification for these unconstitutional methods. These methods are nothing but the Grammar of Anarchy and the sooner they are abandoned, the better for us.

The second thing we must do is to observe the caution which John Stuart Mill has given to all who are interested in the maintenance of democracy, namely, not 'to lay their liberties at the feet of even a great man, or to trust him with powers which enable him to subvert their institutions'. There is nothing wrong in being grateful to great men who have rendered life-long services to the country. But there are limits to gratefulness. In religion, Bhakti may be a road to the salvation of the soul. But in politics, Bhakti or hero-worship is a sure road to degradation and to eventual dictatorship.

The third thing we must do is not to be content with mere political democracy. We must make our political democracy a social democracy as well. Political democracy cannot last unless there lies at the base of it social democracy. What does social democracy mean? It means a way of life which recognizes liberty, equality and fraternity as the principles of life.

On the 26th of January 1950, we are going to enter into a life of contradictions. In politics we will have equality and in social and economic life we will have inequality. In politics we will be recognizing the principle of one man one vote and one vote one value. In our social and economic life, we shall, by reason of our social and economic structure, continue to deny the principle of one man one value. How long shall we continue to live this life of contradictions? How long shall we continue to deny equality in our social and economic life? If we continue to deny it for long, we will do so only by putting our political democracy in peril.
summary: Dr. Ambedkar's historic valedictory speech warning that political democracy ('one man one vote') is unsustainable without social and economic equality ('one man one value'), condemning political hero-worship (Bhakti), and calling for strict constitutional methods.
key_quotes: In politics, Bhakti or hero-worship is a sure road to degradation and to eventual dictatorship.
On 26th January 1950, we are going to enter into a life of contradictions: in politics we will have equality, in social and economic life we will have inequality.
These methods are nothing but the Grammar of Anarchy and the sooner they are abandoned, the better for us.

title: Intervention on the Objectives Resolution
topic: Unity of India, Rights of Minorities, and Statesmanship in Drafting the Fundamental Law
full_text:
Mr. Chairman, I am indeed very grateful to you for giving me this opportunity to express my views on this Resolution. To be candid, I have arrived here with a heavy heart. My mind is full of anxiety about the future of this country. I know today we are divided politically, socially, and economically. We are a group of warring camps and I am probably one of the leaders of such a camp. But, Sir, with all our differences, I am entirely convinced that given time and given goodwill, there is nothing in the world that will prevent this country from becoming one. With all our cultural differences, economic differences and linguistic differences, nothing can prevent people of this country from being one united nation.

Our difficulty is not about the ultimate goal. Our difficulty is how to get together, how to reconcile our differences so that we may march along that road. What I plead for is statesmanship, patience, and mutual accommodation. You cannot force people into a constitutional union by coercion; unity must emerge from justice and voluntary consent of all communities.
summary: Dr. Ambedkar's maiden intervention in the Constituent Assembly urging national unity, goodwill towards minorities, and consensus-building rather than political coercion.
key_quotes: With all our differences, I am entirely convinced that given time and given goodwill, there is nothing in the world that will prevent this country from becoming one.
Unity must emerge from justice and voluntary consent of all communities.

title: Debate on Directive Principles of State Policy
topic: Justiciability and Instrument of Instructions for Governments
full_text:
In enacting this part of the Constitution, the Assembly is giving certain directions to the future legislature and the future executive of this country. If it is said that the Directive Principles have no legal force behind them, I am prepared to admit it. But I am not prepared to admit that they have no binding force at all. Nor am I prepared to concede that they are useless. The Directive Principles are like the Instrument of Instructions which were issued to the Governor-General by the British Government under the 1935 Act.

Whoever captures power will not be free to do what he likes with it. In the exercise of it, he will have to respect these instruments of instructions which are called Directive Principles. He cannot ignore them. He may not have to answer for their breach in a court of law. But he will certainly have to answer for them before the electorate at election times. What great value these principles possess will be realized when we consider that they set the economic direction towards social democracy.
summary: Dr. Ambedkar clarifies the profound significance of Directive Principles of State Policy: though non-justiciable in courts, they are supreme political instructions that every democratically elected government must account for before the people.
key_quotes: Directive Principles are like the Instrument of Instructions... He may not have to answer for their breach in a court of law, but he will certainly have to answer before the electorate.
They set the economic direction towards social democracy.

title: Debate on Untouchability Abolition (Article 17)
topic: Draft Article 11 (Final Article 17): Complete Abolition and Criminalization of Untouchability
full_text:
The Constituent Assembly took up Draft Article 11: 'Untouchability is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden. The enforcement of any disability arising out of Untouchability shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law.'

Dr. Ambedkar strongly championed the immediate constitutional prohibition of untouchability without exceptions or qualifiers. He underscored that civil equality is meaningless if social ostracism and systemic degradation are permitted under the guise of tradition. This article represents a solemn national covenant to eradicate the thousands of years of humiliation inflicted upon the depressed classes. Parliament shall have the exclusive power to enact penal laws under Article 35 to ensure stringent, uniform enforcement across all states.
summary: The landmark debate and unanimous passage of Article 17 of the Indian Constitution, abolishing untouchability and declaring its practice in any form a punishable offense.
key_quotes: Untouchability is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden.
Civil equality is meaningless if systemic degradation is permitted under the guise of custom.

title: Debate on Due Process of Law vs Procedure Established by Law
topic: Draft Article 15 (Final Article 21): Protection of Life and Personal Liberty
full_text:
The question before the House is whether the words should be 'procedure established by law' or 'due process of law'. I must confess that I am in a somewhat difficult position with regard to this amendment. The question of whether we should adopt 'due process' or 'procedure established by law' is one where two contending views exist in constitutional jurisprudence.

If you use 'due process', you give the judiciary the power to question not merely whether a law was enacted according to proper legislative competence and procedure, but also whether the substance of the law is good or bad, just or unjust. On the other hand, if you restrict it to 'procedure established by law', the judiciary is confined to seeing whether the procedure prescribed by the legislature was observed. The House must choose between the supremacy of the legislature and the supremacy of the judiciary. The Drafting Committee placed the matter before the Assembly to make this momentous choice.
summary: Dr. Ambedkar's insightful analysis on Draft Article 15 (now Article 21) examining the delicate constitutional balance between judicial review under 'due process' and legislative prerogative under 'procedure established by law'.
key_quotes: The question is whether you want judicial supremacy or legislative supremacy in evaluating the substantive justice of laws.

title: Debate on Religious Freedom and Social Reform
topic: Draft Article 19 (Final Article 25): Freedom of Conscience and Right to Freely Profess Religion
full_text:
The religious conceptions in this country are so vast that they cover every aspect of life from birth to death. There is nothing which is not religion. If we agree that religious freedom covers all actions claimed as religious, then the legislature would be disabled from enacting any social reform legislation whatsoever.

We must claim the right to separate religious belief and faith from secular activities associated with religion. The State must retain paramount power under Article 25(2) to regulate secular activities and provide for social welfare and reform, including throwing open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of society.
summary: Dr. Ambedkar defends the state's power to legislate social reform and eradicate caste discrimination in religious institutions, demarcating genuine spiritual faith from discriminatory secular practices.
key_quotes: If we agree that religious freedom covers all actions claimed as religious, then the legislature would be disabled from enacting any social reform legislation whatsoever.

title: Debate on Emergency Provisions and Article 356
topic: President's Rule in Case of Failure of Constitutional Machinery in States
full_text:
With regard to Article 356, I do not altogether deny that there is a possibility of these articles being abused or employed for political purposes. But that objection applies to every part of the Constitution which gives discretion to the Executive.

The proper thing we ought to expect is that such articles will never be called into operation and that they would remain a dead letter. If at all they are brought into operation, I hope the President, who is endowed with this power, will take proper precautions before actually suspending the administration of the provinces.
summary: Dr. Ambedkar's renowned doctrine that Article 356 (President's Rule) was conceived as a 'dead letter' to be deployed only as an extreme last resort against genuine breakdown of constitutional order, warning against its partisan misuse.
key_quotes: The proper thing we ought to expect is that such articles will never be called into operation and that they would remain a dead letter.

title: Debate on Uniform Civil Code (Article 44)
topic: Article 35 (Final Article 44): State's Endeavor to Secure a Uniform Civil Code
full_text:
We have in this country a uniform civil code in almost every aspect of civil life except personal laws: we have a uniform law of crimes under the Indian Penal Code, Civil Procedure Code, Transfer of Property Act, Contract Act, and Sale of Goods Act. The only little corner which has remained untouched is personal law relating to marriage and succession.

I do not propose that the State shall immediately enforce a code upon all communities irrespective of their willingness. The article merely declares it to be the duty of the State to endeavor towards it, while providing ample room for voluntary application and evolutionary consensus.
summary: Dr. Ambedkar argues for Article 44 (Uniform Civil Code) in the Directive Principles, demonstrating that India already had unified criminal and commercial codes, advocating progressive alignment through legislative consensus.
key_quotes: We have a uniform law of crimes, property, and contracts throughout India; the only little corner remaining untouched is marriage and succession.

title: Debate on Constitutional Morality and Village Realities
topic: Critique of Village Republics and Elaboration of Constitutional Morality
full_text:
What is the village but a sink of localism, a den of ignorance, narrow-mindedness and communalism? I am glad that the Draft Constitution has discarded the village and adopted the individual as its unit. The Constitution must uphold the dignity and rights of the individual citizen against oppressive local majorities.

Constitutional morality is not a natural sentiment. It has to be cultivated. We must realize that our people have yet to learn it. Democracy in India is only a top-dressing on an Indian soil, which is essentially undemocratic.
summary: Dr. Ambedkar defends taking the individual as the fundamental unit of the Constitution rather than village units, articulating that constitutional morality must be deliberately cultivated in a deeply hierarchical society.
key_quotes: Constitutional morality is not a natural sentiment. It has to be cultivated.
Democracy in India is only a top-dressing on an Indian soil, which is essentially undemocratic.
